title: HABRI Survey Reports Broader Recognition of Pet Ownership and Perceived Health Benefits
description: According to Veterinary Practice News, HABRI’s 2026 U.S. nationwide survey highlighted perceived health benefits felt by pet owners, awareness of the human-animal bond, links to preventive care, and barriers to ownership. However, as a self-reported survey, it did not confirm causation.

sections.heading: What the HABRI survey showed
paragraphs: According to Veterinary Practice News, in the 2026 U.S. nationwide survey by the Human Animal Bond Research Institute (HABRI), a majority of pet owners said they had experienced at least one health benefit. The same article said a majority of Americans reported being aware of research-confirmed benefits.
The report addresses changes in social perceptions of pet ownership and behavioral attitudes, but the responses are based solely on survey participants’ self-reports.

sections.heading: What the numbers indicate
paragraphs: Based on the figures presented in the article alone, emotional benefits such as reduced loneliness and lower stress emerged as the most readily recognized items. There were also many responses saying that, after learning about human-animal bond research, they spent more time with their pets and took better care of their health.
However, these results are responses that people ‘felt that way’ in a survey; they do not prove how much actual health improvement there was.

sections.heading: Practical points for the pet industry
paragraphs: Domestic Korean pet businesses need to separately verify how owners’ perceptions are linked to actual visits, repeat visits, and the maintenance of vaccinations when designing preventive care and daily-care guidance.

In addition, because cost and housing restrictions are often cited as barriers to pet ownership, it is advisable to take these real-world constraints into account in service design and 상담 materials as well.

takeaway: This report shows the perceived benefits of pet ownership and public awareness, but its limitation as a self-reported survey is clear.
Korean readers should not generalize the U.S. survey results as-is, and should verify them again using domestic owner data and on-the-ground responses.
From a FOURFEETZ perspective, the key point is not simply ‘bonding,’ but whether that perception actually leads to preventive care behavior, which needs separate verification.
